That separates them from philosophers in the proper sense. Philosophers, without exception, believe that all questions that can be asked follow logically and necessarily from one another. It is enough to ask the first question suggested to a human being by his life, and from there either we can eventually reach the final question, as some philosophers believe, or we can go on progressing forever, as others maintain.
We must not imagine that this distinction between anthropological philosophy and theological pseudo-philosophy is the same as the distinction within philosophy between theism and atheism.
As we will now see, that second distinction comes down to whether one denies or accepts the possibility that a human being can attain wisdom.
It is true—and the word itself makes this obvious—that theological systems are usually also theistic. But this is not necessarily always the case, and there are exceptions.

If we call “god” whatever principle revelation supposedly comes from, then we can certainly say that every theological system contains some concept of god. But the word “god” then becomes unusually broad and vague.

It is difficult, for example, to say what exactly corresponds to “god” in early Buddhism, and it is far more natural to describe early Buddhism as atheistic. Yet it undeniably has a theological character in the sense just defined.

The same is true of “mystics,” ancient and modern, who work with ideas such as “inspiration,” “presence,” “intuition,” and so on. Strictly speaking, they cannot all be counted as theists, even though their openly declared theological orientation is beyond doubt.
In any case, the distinction that matters here concerns neither the object nor the goal of philosophy. It concerns its method.
Where “revelation” comes from—god or something else not ordinarily called god, such as the “subconscious”—is not the issue.
The issue is whether one recognizes revelation itself.

If someone believes that not all questions can be asked or all answers given without some kind of revelation, then that person belongs to the camp of theological pseudo-philosophy, opposed to philosophy in the proper sense.
We can therefore formulate the distinction as follows.

We can speak of “revelation” whenever certain questions or answers are not available to everyone, or whenever they require some special sui generis state unrelated to the normal development of discourse.

Alongside the familiar theology of theists, for whom revelation comes from god, we therefore find atheistic religions such as Buddhism, in which revelation comes from exceptional or specially gifted persons—“sages,” “saints,” and so on.
And we also find a nonreligious “mysticism” in which revelation is in principle available to everyone, but only under certain special and irrational conditions such as “ecstasy.”
On the other hand, philosophy in the proper sense is by no means always atheistic.

Theism is an error, as we will later try to show. But an error can still be philosophical, and experience shows that a thinker can arrive—mistakenly, but by an entirely philosophical method—at a concept of god indistinguishable from a similar theological or religious concept.

What matters is only that questions and answers concerning god should in principle be available to anyone capable of rational speech and in a normal, conscious state. Discourse about god must be logically connected with discourse about humanity and the world.
We must therefore distinguish atheistic or theistic philosophy from atheistic or theistic theology.
And the problem of these two kinds of philosophy brings us back to the question we raised earlier and postponed: can wisdom be attained?
What does it mean to say that human beings cannot attain wisdom?

Socrates already seems to have claimed that wisdom was inaccessible—or at least that is how his disciple Plato presents him. By examining Plato’s philosophy, we can see what this means and what follows from it.

Suppose we ask someone why he refrains from murder, even when his “instinct” might push him toward it. He answers: because human life has the highest value and must never be sacrificed for the sake of any other value.
Naturally, we immediately ask another question: why do you regard human life as the highest value?
Now suppose that no one can ever answer that question.

In that case, the first answer also becomes unsatisfactory. The person does not really know why he refrains from killing. His refusal to kill is not rational. Two “instincts” are simply struggling inside him, and that is all.
He could therefore never convince someone who said the opposite: that killing is permissible.
What applies here applies everywhere else.

Because philosophical questions, unlike theological ones, are all logically connected with one another, once we claim that some of them must forever remain unanswered, we undermine the certainty and persuasive force—the “rationality”—of every answer already given.

And this position inevitably leads, as it has repeatedly done in history, to theoretical skepticism, moral nihilism, and political and social anarchism. It makes philosophy itself, and even social and public life, impossible.
If we want to avoid this conclusion—and every philosopher must want to avoid it—then we have to say something like the following.

Perhaps the human being, as a speaking creature living in a material world of space and time, cannot answer the final question. But the answer nevertheless exists outside humanity, in some nonhuman being that also possesses logos, the capacity for meaningful speech, part of whose discourse coincides with human discourse.
The individual philosopher will never become a sage.

But there is a nonhuman sage, and the philosopher’s partial knowledge is genuine because it partially coincides with the complete knowledge of this sage, who can continue where the philosopher stops and answer the questions that arise after the philosopher has gone as far as he can.
Such a nonhuman sage may be called the philosopher’s god.

Any philosophy that regards itself merely as philo-sophy—as a pursuit of wisdom that does not actually reach its goal—must therefore presuppose the existence of a sage outside the circle of human philosophers.
In philosophical terms, it must be theistic.
This is precisely how Plato understood the matter.

He wanted to avoid the nihilism of the Sophists without claiming that human beings could actually attain wisdom. He therefore deliberately introduced the concept of god into his philosophy as the “ultimate guarantee of truth,” an expression we later encounter in Descartes.
But although Plato became a theist, he remained a philosopher, because he did not take the theological path of revelation.

He insists strongly that whatever questions and answers we may have about ourselves are available to everyone, and that these questions are asked and answered in the ordinary state in which he conducted all his other rational conversations.
There may indeed be some questions that human beings can never answer. But every answer they do give, they give themselves. And where they are unable to answer, no “revelation” comes to their rescue.
It is very difficult to say why Plato denied that wisdom could be attained. Perhaps we have reached an ultimate and irreducible irrational attitude.

But we should note—especially once we see everything implied by the concept of wisdom—that from a psychological point of view there is nothing surprising about Plato and most other philosophers denying that wisdom can be reached.
What should surprise us, psychologically speaking, is the extraordinary intellectual boldness of those philosophers who claimed that it could.
In any case, it fell to Aristotle—Plato’s greatest and closest disciple—to defend the possibility of attaining wisdom.
We cannot say with certainty that Aristotle regarded himself as a “sage.” But there is no doubt that, unlike his teacher, he believed wisdom was in principle attainable by a human being.
A simple example will make this position clear.
Today, very few people could tell you the exact digit in the 100,000th decimal place of the number π. It is possible that no one will ever in fact know it.
But in principle, the digit can be calculated.
And if that is so, then even without carrying out the entire calculation ourselves, we can still say that all the already known decimal digits involved in it are absolutely correct.
The truth of mathematics in general rests on the same principle.
The same can be said of any chain of questions and answers.

It is precisely because a human being can in principle answer any question, always using the same human means, that the answers already given—and only those answers—can be true without our having to assume the existence of some wisdom outside humanity.
In other words, Aristotle’s philosophical position makes it unnecessary for him to introduce the philosophical concept of god as a guarantee of truth.
What we have said makes the logical connection clear.
To deny that wisdom can be attained leads to philosophical theism.
To affirm that wisdom is attainable can—and should—lead us to atheism.
Descartes, for example, denied that wisdom could be attained and explicitly introduced god as the sole guarantee of truth.
Spinoza, by contrast, regarded wisdom as attainable and in practice denied god, even though he speaks about “god” on almost every page—deceiving no one except perhaps himself.

Later, Kant constructed his entire “critical” philosophy in order to prove that the limits of our knowledge could never be crossed. He explicitly said that the purpose of his philosophy was to clear a space for belief in god.
Hegel, by contrast, explicitly and insistently affirmed that wisdom was possible, and regarded himself as a “sage.” He therefore appeared as a radical atheist.
We can thus distinguish two fundamental and opposing currents within philosophy, as distinct from theology.

The first, necessarily theistic, holds that in any chain of questions and answers we eventually reach a point beyond which we cannot go, at least so long as a human being remains fully human—that is, so long as he lives on earth. Some versions of this view allow wisdom to be attained after death.

The second, atheistic in principle, holds that there are no such impassable limits, and that a human being can, at least in theory, answer every possible question while remaining human—that is, while using ordinary human speech here on earth.
But within this second current we can once again distinguish two basic positions.
Some believe that wisdom can be acquired by an isolated individual, regardless of the conditions in which that individual lives.
Others believe it can be attained only once the right conditions of collective life have been created.
We will later see that the atheistic claim that wisdom is accessible is the only correct one, but that its individualistic version is mistaken.
In other words, if we claim that wisdom must be attained by an isolated individual, whatever his circumstances, then Plato is right to say that this is impossible.
Where Plato is wrong is in claiming that wisdom remains impossible under every possible set of conditions.

Plato, Aristotle, and pagan philosophy in general—and indeed nearly all philosophers in every age—believed that only the isolated thinker, withdrawn from the world and from other people, could and should seek wisdom, that is, become a philosopher.
Hegel alone understood that if we pose the problem in this way, we are inevitably forced into one of two positions.
Either we contradict ourselves by claiming that wisdom has already been attained, or at least can be attained, and thereby fall into error.
Or we deny that it can be attained.

But once we make that denial, we are just as inevitably led either—in the best case—to ground wisdom in god and thereby preserve the rationality of human life, or else to appeal to various forms of “revelation,” or finally, at the last stage of philosophical decline, to deny that intelligible and convincing answers are possible at all and drown in the boundless sea of nihilistic and skeptical anarchism.
In reality, all these consequences can be avoided if we assume that wisdom is ultimately attainable only through the collective effort of humanity, and only at a particular stage of that effort.
Only this position is compatible with genuine philosophy: philosophy that is neither theological nor theistic.
Hegel’s great achievement was precisely to understand this and to demonstrate it, breaking with all his predecessors.
We should add, however, that Hegel’s solution was prepared in a rather strange way—not by pagan and atheistic philosophy, but by Christian, theological, and theistic pseudo-philosophy.

As we will later see, it was within Jewish and Christian thought that the idea first appeared of truth developing historically, and of its revelation by humanity having a collective or communal character.

We can say that Hegel simply removed the theological and theistic shell from an idea that was correct in its core, assigning to the State and to humanity what Christianity had assigned to the Church and to god.

In any case, Hegel’s solution—which is in fact the only possible solution—to the problem of wisdom and the pursuit of wisdom, that is, philosophy, passed directly from Hegel into Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, which today is the only genuine successor to Hegelian thought.
It is this Hegelian-Marxist conception of genuine philosophy—that is, philosophy which is neither theological nor theistic—that we must now examine.
When the socialist revolution began in Russia, the adjective “conscious” immediately achieved extraordinary popularity.

Expressions such as “I am conscious,” “the conscious proletariat,” “you conscious citizens,” and so on could be heard on every street corner. Even when our enemies used the word mockingly, our friends pronounced it with conviction and enthusiasm.
No one doubted that what was meant was the revolutionary conscious awareness of the masses.
But after the revolution had won, the idea of conscious awareness was not discarded.

On the contrary, the Party and the government continued to orient themselves ideologically toward the revolutionarily conscious masses, to rely on them in action, and to draw their own strength from them.
And while the Party and government tried, on the one hand, to make use of the conscious awareness that had already developed, they also worked, quite naturally, to broaden and deepen it.
Indeed, we can add that this work of extending and deepening conscious awareness has never been carried out with greater consciousness than in our present Stalinist era.

Finally, it can be shown that the ideal of conscious awareness is closely connected with the ideal of communist society, which from the Marxist-Leninist-Stalinist point of view is humanity’s ultimate ideal.
On the one hand, this ideal can clearly be fully realized only if conscious awareness extends to every citizen and is fully developed in each of them.

On the other hand, once the basic technical and economic problems have been solved, once class struggle has finally disappeared, and with it political life in the ordinary sense—and even, if one wishes, “historical” life in its precommunist sense—then this same conscious awareness, its consolidation, expansion, and deepening, will become the fundamental content of communist human existence.
In a communist society, where everyone is able to live according to their needs, it is natural that human effort will be directed less toward simply living than toward living consciously.

How, then, should we understand this “conscious awareness” which gives rise to socialist revolution, feeds on the revolution as it develops, nourishes that development in turn, and ultimately seeks to spread universally and develop completely?

We only have to ask the question and think about it for a moment to see that the revolutionary and socialist concept of “conscious awareness” coincides with the philosophical concept of self-consciousness.
